2-s2.0-85073358398.other: Critical political economy of digital technology (Fuchs, digital capitalism)
2-s2.0-85073358398.notes: Theoretical essay with teaching proposals for schools and universities that were not implemented. No specific level. It reviews literature as part of the argument, not as a review.

2-s2.0-85068434540.notes: Video production workshop with 40 pre-service elementary teachers (Canada). Visual ethnography; pre and post questionnaires reported as percentages, with no comparison group. Framework: New Literacies and multiliteracies, and critical literacy 'in the Freirean sense'.

2-s2.0-85178434081.notes: In practice CDL is reduced to judging the credibility of online sources (SIFT method, COVID-19 fake news). The framework cites critical pedagogy, but tasks and results do not address power: 'discuss the distinction between credible and non-credible online sources' (p. 1). Borderline case, excluded under Table 1 (critical = checking the reliability of a source). COIL intervention with 8 pre-service foreign language teachers.

2-s2.0-85144350861.other: Social semiotics in second language acquisition (Kramsch, Bourdieu); CDL after Darvin
2-s2.0-85144350861.notes: Six-week virtual exchange between pre-service English teachers (Turkey) and master's students (UK); thematic analysis of 37 portfolios. Internet censorship in China appears in one group only, and the article itself says the tasks did not steer towards social justice: the infrastructural dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-85174682656.notes: Theoretical and methodological proposal for critical media literacy from the political economy of communication: a worksheet for analysing mass media news ('structural hemerography'). The digital is marginal (mentions of social media, clickbait), so it is not CDL as defined in the review. Borderline case: it addresses power and media ownership, but of mass media.

2-s2.0-85089543383.notes: Online questionnaire with 322 pre-service primary teachers (five Spanish universities): analysis of digital news with a rubric; results as percentages by level. Diagnostic, no intervention. Framework: Freirean critical pedagogy and critical media literacy (Kellner and Share).

2-s2.0-85185907678.notes: Teaching sequence of 7-8 hours on political speech in upper secondary school (Greece), with Voyant, posters and videos. It reports having been taught but presents no data. Borderline eligibility: the digital is mostly a tool; included because it analyses power in online audiovisual texts. Production (posters, speeches) practises persuasion rather than seeking change: the transformative dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-105044863875.other: Social studies of technology and political economy of platforms (Winner, Pötzsch, Zuboff)
2-s2.0-105044863875.notes: Deductive qualitative content analysis of the official Spanish lower secondary curriculum (Royal Decree 217/2022) with three CDL dimensions (texts, artefacts, infrastructure) very close to the review's. All three dimensions are categories of the study's analysis.

2-s2.0-85191972621.other: Critical thinking (Ennis); CDL as a recommended perspective
2-s2.0-85191972621.notes: Systematic review (49 Web of Science studies, 2012-2021) of critical thinking and social media in education. Borderline case: the object is critical thinking, with CDL as a perspective and a conclusion. Included because it defines the critical as grasping ideology and intent. Covers all levels without focusing on one.

2-s2.0-105044792238.other: Critical theory of technology (Feenberg); open educational practices; agency for learning
2-s2.0-105044792238.notes: Web scraping and content analysis of the websites of 84 Spanish universities on critical digital competence, agency and open education (303 records). The infrastructural dimension is the yardstick for judging what is found. Record frequencies are descriptive: the quantitative design is not coded.

2-s2.0-105040530988.notes: Phenomenology with 9 Arab bilingual university students writing in English with generative AI (UAE). Explicit decolonial framework. Sentiment scores summarise the qualitative coding: the quantitative design is not coded. No intervention.

2-s2.0-105040212695.other: CDL after Darvin (2025); decolonial writing pedagogy (Canagarajah)
2-s2.0-105040212695.notes: Qualitative case study (one pre-service English teacher, Indonesia) with photovoice, interviews and AI use logs, within a course with tasks designed by the author. The framework cites the political economy of AI (Darvin), but tasks and findings do not examine infrastructure: the infrastructural dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-105043711991.notes: Survey of 3,086 university students in five countries on the need to regulate ChatGPT and its ethical risks (plagiarism, cheating, privacy), compared by gender. CDL appears only as a closing recommendation ('promote critical digital literacy with a gender perspective', p. 15); the study does not analyse texts or infrastructures in terms of power. Borderline case: if eligible it would be higher education, quantitative, evaluation 0, object AI.

2-s2.0-105036421715.other: CDL as its own framework (Pangrazio and Selwyn; Darvin; Hinrichsen and Coombs; Mihailidis)
2-s2.0-105036421715.notes: Interviews and digital diaries with 13 Iranian university students learning English on Instagram. The learning studied is informal, but participants are university students and the implications are addressed to the formal curriculum: considered eligible (borderline on context). 'Digital agency' is individual (choosing or rejecting content): the transformative dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-85146978440.other: Own CDL framework (Gouseti et al., 2021), with Pötzsch (2019) and Nichols and Stornaiuolo
2-s2.0-85146978440.notes: Focus groups with in-service primary and secondary teachers in four countries (Erasmus+ project). Teachers' perceptions centre on safety, sources and technical use; analysis of representation and power does not appear. The authors introduce the infrastructural dimension when they point to the absence of data literacy. Co-creation and reinventing media are in the framework, but the findings show they are not practised: the transformative dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-105028754138.notes: Mixed-methods study with 170 Chilean engineering students on AI adoption, perceived usefulness and ambivalence (self-determination theory). CDL appears only in the abstract and conclusions as an institutional recommendation (p. 1 and p. 14); texts and infrastructures are not analysed in terms of power.

2-s2.0-105019658839.other: CDL model of Cajavilca et al. (2025): technological socialisation and the sequence denaturalise–problematise–propose (Monarca et al., 2023); Pötzsch
2-s2.0-105019658839.notes: Content analysis of 33 portfolios of university students (psychology, criminology, engineering) acting as mentors in the EducamosContigo programme; the CDL module (Block I) was taught and the portfolios are analysed as evidence of learning. The infrastructural and transformative dimensions are categories of analysis (structural problematisation and proposals), although the results show they hardly appear (proposals: 1.5%). Percentages are counts of coded references: 'quantitative' is not coded. The programme mixes formal and non-formal education.

2-s2.0-85112660754.notes: Online questionnaire with 250 upper secondary students: they interpret two tweets with false or biased information (gender violence, LGBTIQ+, Francoism); narratives are classified with a rubric and reported as percentages. Framework: reading the word and the world (Freire and Macedo) and education for critical citizenship. Social transformation appears only as a general orientation: the transformative dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-105053839720.notes: Descriptive quantitative study with 70 first-year Indonesian university students who respond in writing to three problematic texts (a health hoax, a biased headline, a narrative of distrust in the media). CDL is operationalised as credibility evaluation, verification, reasoning and awareness of bias, understood as sensationalism or one-sided presentation; power, ideology and platforms are not analysed (one mention of 'ideological framing' in the introduction, p. 1). Same criterion as Ketzer-Nöltge 2022: 'critical' reduces to judging reliability. Borderline, because the title and framework are declared as CDL.

2-s2.0-105032656699.other: CDL after Macgilchrist (2021); Foucault and semiocapitalism (Berardi)
2-s2.0-105032656699.notes: Multiple case study with seven Galician adolescents aged 14 to 17 (observation of Instagram profiles and interviews), recruited through schools; the implications are addressed to schools. The feminist framework is adopted as the framework (gender as a power-knowledge device). 'Surveillance' is coded for self-surveillance, the central theme. 'Production' because the practice studied is posting one's own images. The transformative dimension is a closing proposal for schools, not documented practice.

2-s2.0-105032689737.other: Studies of educational platformisation (van Dijck, Williamson, Pangrazio and Selwyn) and sociology of childhood (children's agency)
2-s2.0-105032689737.notes: Focus groups with pupils aged 10 to 12 and an ethnographic case study in Catalonia on protection and support in platformised schools. CDL is the lens of the discussion and platformisation the framework; considered eligible because it addresses the infrastructural dimension (borderline: the declared focus is protection). The transformative dimension is coded for the proposal that pupils take part in choosing the school's digital tools, which the authors note is absent from the findings (a proposal, not documented practice).

2-s2.0-105043359807.other: Neuroeducation and cultural studies (Giroux, McLaren and Kincheloe)
2-s2.0-105043359807.notes: Theoretical-critical essay based on a narrative review: proposes the 'TikTok brain' to think about attention and learning in algorithmic culture, with critical pedagogy as one of three pillars and CDL in the curricular proposals. Borderline eligibility: the main object is cognitive effects; the infrastructural dimension appears in the framework and the textual one only as a description of critical media literacy. Refers to 'young people' and 'students' in general: no level.

2-s2.0-85146934143.other: Postdigital perspective and critique of datafication (Selwyn and Jandrić; surveillance and platform capitalism)
2-s2.0-85146934143.notes: Replacement, 2020–2023. Case study of a four-session sequence in a compulsory first-year module of primary teacher education: teams evaluate tools with a rubric (privacy, data ownership, accessibility) and build their own rating scale; ePortfolio reflections are analysed. Markham ('pedagogy of the digitally oppressed') is cited in passing: critical pedagogy is not coded. Building the rating scale is critical evaluation, not production of alternatives: the transformative dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-85198736078.notes: Replacement, 2020–2023. Redesign of a writing module for computing students in Singapore with Hinrichsen and Coombs's five-resources model: an online commentary on a digital text, with pre and post perception surveys. 'Critical' means general critical thinking (Ennis; Paul and Elder: clarity, precision, logic) and argumentation; ideology is mentioned once (p. 5). Same criterion as the codebook rule on generic critical thinking. Borderline: if eligible it would be higher education, intervention and quantitative, evaluation 2, no dimensions.

2-s2.0-85176211357.other: Critical data literacy and data justice (Dencik, Taylor); open educational practices
2-s2.0-85176211357.notes: Replacement, 2020–2023. Eight professional development courses for academics (and some public officials) in Latin America, 2016–2022, using open data as educational resources; self-assessment of competences at the start and end, with no comparison group. The feminist framework (D'Ignazio and Klein, hooks) and active citizenship are adopted as the framework. Coded as teacher education because participants are university teachers.

2-s2.0-85120359325.notes: Replacement, 2020–2023. Design-based research: a four-month critical media literacy programme with 29 upper secondary students (aged 14–15) at a teacher-training secondary school in Colombia; this article reports only the Alfamed questionnaire before and after (Wilcoxon), with no comparison group. The infrastructural dimension rests on the Cambridge Analytica case and on the relations between corporate media power and messages (p. 3). Participants produce videos without aiming at change: the transformative dimension is not coded. The first PDF retrieved (from an institutional repository) was a different article; the journal's own PDF was used.

2-s2.0-105053382404.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Psychometric validation of an AI literacy scale (3wAI) with 546 adult learners at a distance university in Turkey. The 'critical' dimension of the scale consists of general ethical beliefs ('I believe it is important to use AI technologies responsibly', p. 11); CDL appears only as a keyword. Texts and infrastructures are not analysed in terms of power. If eligible it would be higher education, quantitative, evaluation 0, object AI.

2-s2.0-105046344766.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Quasi-experiment with a control group (48 immigrant secondary students learning Spanish) on generative AI as a semiotic mediator in multimodal tasks, from multiliteracies. 'Critical digital literacy' reduces to checking the reliability, provenance and attribution of generated content (p. 10); representations and infrastructures are not analysed in terms of power. Borderline: if eligible it would be secondary, qualitative, quantitative and intervention, evaluation 3, multiliteracies, objects AI, foreign languages and production.

2-s2.0-105013271101.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Eight-week mixed-methods intervention with 35 university English majors in Thailand: ChatGPT as support for critical reading (pre and post tests, questionnaire, interviews). 'Critical' refers to critical reading skills (evaluating arguments, recognising bias and tone, counterarguing); the cultural bias of AI is mentioned only in the framework (p. 6). Same criterion as the rule on generic critical thinking. Borderline: if eligible it would be higher education, qualitative, quantitative and intervention, evaluation 2, objects AI and foreign languages.

2-s2.0-105011296978.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Critical narrative analysis (interviews, focus groups, reflections) with BIPOC pre-service teachers at a historically Black university in the United States on access to technology, self-efficacy and intended use (sociocultural theory and theory of planned behaviour). The object is the digital divide and technology integration; CDL appears only in the recommendations (p. 2 and p. 16).

2-s2.0-105044002015.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Interviews with 12 Spanish university teachers on 24 open educational practices, analysed with the CoDiCri ACAD toolkit; the focus is the design of the learning setting (spaces, tools, OER). Critical digital competence is defined with reference to power (p. 2), but the analysis shows only general elements (critical thinking about the digital world, citizenship, evaluating content) without addressing representations or infrastructures. Borderline, from the same project as Esteve-Mon 2026 (eligible because it uses the infrastructural dimension as a criterion of analysis). If eligible: higher education, qualitative, evaluation 0, no dimensions.

2-s2.0-105028561569.other: Critical digital pedagogy; inclusive education and the critique of deficit thinking
2-s2.0-105028561569.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Critical action research across three cohorts of an initial teacher education course in Australia (60 participants, 12 weeks): lesson planning with AI, analysis of 123 plans, journals, focus groups and pre and post surveys with inferential statistics (no comparison group). Freire is the declared framework. The infrastructural dimension is not coded: the study analyses the bias of the recommendations, not how the tool works or whose interests it serves. The transformative dimension is coded because participants redesign their differentiation practices to resist the bias.

2-s2.0-105053728805.other: Semiotics and intersemiotic translation (Jakobson); multimodal translation
2-s2.0-105053728805.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Classroom workshop with 34 Greek translation students: they translate into Greek the posters of a UNICEF campaign against cyberbullying, and their choices are analysed as signs of critical awareness. Critical pedagogy (Freire) and digital citizenship are presented in the framework. The cyberbullying in the campaign is not discriminatory: hate speech is not coded. Foreign languages because it is set in translator education (English-Greek).

2-s2.0-105003655871.other: Sociotechnical and critical studies of technology (Zuboff, Morozov); hermeneutic-critical paradigm
2-s2.0-105003655871.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Critical glossary of 40 terms on AI and metaverses built through content analysis of recent literature (four axes, one sociotechnical: algocracy, data capitalism, extractivism, surveillance). Coded as a review. Borderline eligibility: the object is terminology and CDL is the proposed use; considered eligible because it addresses the infrastructural dimension. The textual dimension is coded for its critique of techno-pedagogical discourse (same criterion as Pötzsch 2019). No specific level.

2-s2.0-85189013690.other: Service learning and online social capital
2-s2.0-85189013690.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Survey of 416 pre-service early childhood teachers in Taiwan analysed with partial least squares: relations between service learning, self-reported CDL and online social capital. Cross-sectional, does not evaluate an intervention (evaluation 0). CDL is the central construct and is defined in terms of power and ideology, although the items are general ('I can identify and analyze bias in news articles and online content', p. 7). 'Social action' is in the definition but not studied: the transformative dimension is not coded.

2-s2.0-105038382264.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026 (HTML text, no page numbers). Interpretative phenomenological analysis of interviews with ten Thai university students on using social media to learn English, with the digital literacies framework of Dudeney et al. Critical literacy is one of four domains and amounts to judging credibility and managing distraction; power and ideology are not analysed. Unlike Javahery 2026, CDL is not the central framework.

2-s2.0-105032117820.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Systematic review (PRISMA) and meta-analysis of 26 studies on educational uses of TikTok in South America; the aims are to map trends and quantify learning gains. Critical media literacy is one pillar of the framework and a sub-theme of the synthesis (commercial and algorithmic logics, p. 14), but not the focus. Borderline, comparable to Pattier 2026, which was included as a theoretical-critical essay. If eligible: review, no level, objects social media and platforms, infrastructural dimension.

2-s2.0-85188308571.other: Pragmatics: implicit content and presuppositions (Lombardi Vallauri, Sbisà)
2-s2.0-85188308571.notes: Replacement, 2024–2026. Materials for English as a foreign language in upper secondary school (analysing presuppositions in political tweets and advertisements), evaluated in interviews by ten in-service teachers in Austria and Italy. The materials were not taught to students: intervention is not coded. Coded as teacher education because participants are teachers.
